items.scenario: Your contract-review service hard-codes one Claude model ID in 14 files. A deprecation notice for that model arrives, giving a retirement date two months out.
items.question: What is the most robust response?
options: Keep the current model until the retirement date passes, then switch every file to the newest model in one commit
Centralise the model ID in config, run the golden-set regression on the replacement, canary, then cut over early
Switch every file to the replacement ID today and rely on the vendor's statement that quality is equal or better
Switch now and ask users to report any quality drop, rolling back if complaints exceed an agreed threshold
items.explanation: Pinning is only safe with a migration plan: one config point, an eval set that proves the replacement, a canary, and a cutover before retirement (retired models return 404).
distractors: Waiting for the date turns retirement into an outage, because the old ID starts returning errors and the switch is untested.
Switching blind skips the regression; behaviour differences (effort defaults, thinking, prefill) can break the service.
Using users as the test suite means discovering regressions in production, and a rollback target that is retiring anyway.

items.scenario: A nightly job summarises tickets. Some summaries are cut off mid-sentence, and the downstream parser crashes on half-written JSON.
items.question: What should the integration do first?
options: Wrap the parser in a try/except, skip any summary that fails to parse, and report the skipped count weekly
Lower the effort level so that responses come back shorter and fit comfortably inside the existing limit
Check stop_reason and treat max_tokens as a truncated reply: raise the limit or continue, but never parse it
Add 'never exceed the length limit' to the system prompt so the model learns to self-truncate neatly
items.explanation: stop_reason tells you why generation ended. max_tokens means the output is incomplete, so it must never be parsed as a finished answer. Handle it explicitly.
distractors: Silently skipping hides data loss: the job reports success while dropping tickets.
Effort changes reasoning depth, not a guaranteed output length, and doesn't fix the missing stop_reason check.
max_tokens is a hard ceiling the model doesn't see, so a prompt instruction can't make truncation safe.

items.scenario: After upgrading the SDK to a new major version, every call from a data team's classifier fails with HTTP 400. The code sets temperature=0 'for determinism'.
items.question: What is the right fix?
options: Pin the SDK back to the previous major version permanently, so the temperature setting keeps working
Retry the 400 responses with exponential backoff, because the API may simply be under heavy load
Set temperature to its documented default value, so the request passes the new parameter validation
Remove the parameter; get consistency from instructions, examples and structured outputs instead
items.explanation: Sampling parameters were removed in the current API version that new SDK majors send. Remove them, and get consistency through prompt and format controls.
distractors: Pinning an old SDK to keep a removed parameter postpones the problem and blocks every other upgrade.
A 400 is deterministic: the same request fails the same way. Retrying wastes spend.
The parameters are rejected outright, even at their default values.

items.scenario: A support bot sends a 9,000-token system prompt (product docs plus style guide) on every request. The first line of that prompt is 'Current time: {now}'. Cache reads in usage are always zero.
items.question: Why isn't caching working, and what's the fix?
options: Caching only applies to batch requests, so the bot should move its traffic onto the Message Batches API
The timestamp makes every prompt prefix unique; move volatile values to after the cached prefix instead
The system prompt is too long to cache; split it into several smaller requests that each fit the cache
Caching only activates with the 1-hour TTL, so set the ttl field to 1h on the system prompt block
items.explanation: The cache keys on the exact prefix. One changing byte early on invalidates everything after it. Put stable content first and volatile content last, then confirm with usage.cache_read_input_tokens.
distractors: Caching works on ordinary synchronous requests; batching is a separate discount.
Long stable prompts are exactly what caching is for. Length isn't the problem.
The TTL controls lifetime, not activation. With the timestamp in front, nothing would ever be read back.

items.scenario: You need to label 600,000 historical support tickets for a quarterly trend report due in two weeks. Nobody waits on any single result.
items.question: Which approach fits best?
options: Submit them through the Message Batches API, keying every request and result by its custom_id
Send them synchronously in parallel worker threads, as fast as the rate limits will allow
Paste them into a long chat in the app, 500 at a time, and copy the labels out into a sheet
Use the OpenAI compatibility layer, because the existing scripts already target that interface
items.explanation: Non-urgent bulk work is what Batches is for: half price and asynchronous. Results arrive in any order, so key them by custom_id.
distractors: Synchronous calls pay full price and fight rate limits for work that doesn't need low latency.
Manual chat batches are slow and error-prone, and the output can't be reproduced or audited.
The compatibility layer is for testing and comparison, not production workloads, and it lacks features such as caching.

items.scenario: A product manager wants to know whether a 1,200-page technical archive will fit a request, and reaches for a popular open-source tokenizer from another vendor to count it.
items.question: What should you recommend?
options: Use the other vendor's tokenizer, since all modern tokenizers agree to within about one percent
Estimate at four characters per token, which is close enough for a capacity decision like this
Call the token-counting endpoint for that exact model, since only Claude's tokenizer counts its tokens
Send the full request anyway and read the error message back if it turns out to be too large
items.explanation: Token counts depend on the model's tokenizer. The count_tokens endpoint gives the real figure before you spend anything.
distractors: Different tokenizers can differ a lot on the same text, so counts don't carry over between vendors.
A rule of thumb is fine for a first guess, but this is a capacity decision. Use the exact count.
Trial and error costs money and time, and a request that fits can still be close enough to the limit to break later.

items.scenario: Legal wants an internal tool that answers questions about 300-page vendor contracts. They insist on checking every answer against the source before relying on it.
items.question: Which API design best supports that?
options: Return answers as structured JSON with a 'confidence' field, and only show those scoring above 0.9
Raise effort to max on every question, so answers are accurate enough that checking is unnecessary
Summarise each contract first, then answer from the summary so that every request stays small
Enable citations on the document block, and show the cited passages with page numbers per answer
items.explanation: Citations make each answer checkable against the exact source passage, which is what the reviewer needs. Self-reported confidence and higher effort don't replace evidence.
distractors: A model's self-reported confidence isn't calibrated evidence, and citations can't be combined with structured output anyway.
Higher effort can improve answers but never removes the need to verify contract statements.
Answering from a summary drops detail and removes the link back to the clause, the opposite of what legal asked for.

items.scenario: An enterprise client requires all AI traffic to run through their cloud provider's account. Your design relies on the Files API and Message Batches.
items.question: What should you do at design time?
options: Assume full parity with the first-party API, since every route serves the same Claude models
Check that platform's feature-availability table, and plan workarounds for gaps before committing
Proxy calls from the client's cloud account to the first-party API so that you keep every feature
Drop the cloud requirement, because first-party features should take priority over client constraints
items.explanation: Cloud routes have documented feature gaps that change over time. Check availability for the exact platform first, and design workarounds (your own queue, inline documents) before you build.
distractors: Same models doesn't mean same features. Several API features are missing on partner-operated routes.
Routing around the client's mandated platform breaks the contractual requirement the route exists to satisfy.
The client's platform constraint is a requirement. You adapt the design, not the contract.

items.scenario: A long-running triage assistant needs to switch into 'incident communications mode' partway through a conversation. The team plans to rewrite the top-level system prompt on that turn. The conversation's large prefix is cached.
items.question: What is the better approach, and why?
options: Rewrite the top-level system prompt on that turn, since the cache adapts to small edits automatically
Start a brand-new conversation with a new system prompt and no history, as earlier turns aren't needed
Append a mid-conversation system message after the latest user turn; the cached prefix stays intact
Put the new instruction inside an assistant message, so the model reads it as part of its own plan
items.explanation: Editing the top-level system prompt changes the start of the prefix and invalidates the cache for the whole history. A mid-conversation system message adds operator instructions at the end, keeping the cache. Support varies by model and platform, so check it.
distractors: The cache matches exact prefixes. Any edit to the system prompt invalidates everything after it.
Discarding history loses the incident context the assistant needs to write accurate communications.
Putting operator instructions in assistant turns blurs who said what, and prefill-style tricks are rejected on current models.

items.scenario: A request to a current model returns HTTP 200 with stop_reason 'refusal'. The calling service reads content as normal and posts it to a customer-facing channel.
items.question: What should the service do instead?
options: Branch on stop_reason before reading content: log the refusal, then fall back or return a handled message
Retry the identical request immediately until it succeeds, because refusals are usually transient
Treat any HTTP 200 as success, because genuine errors always come back with a 4xx or 5xx status
Increase max_tokens, because refusals happen when the model runs out of room to finish its answer
items.explanation: A refusal comes back with HTTP 200, so status codes alone aren't enough. Check stop_reason first and handle refusal explicitly: log it, use a fallback path, or show a clear message.
distractors: Re-sending the same request usually produces the same refusal, and blind retries waste spend.
Refusals arrive with HTTP 200 by design, so trusting the status code alone posts declined output as an answer.
Refusals come from safety classifiers, not the token limit. A higher max_tokens changes nothing.
